label: thm:deterministic_limit
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Almost sure convergence of $\mathbf Z_t$

title: Proof
body_md:
The reinforcement assumptions imply
$\sum_j|\widetilde A_{ji}|\leq1$ for every $i$.
Hence, in the induced matrix $1$-norm,
\[
\|WQ\widetilde A\|_1
\leq
\|W\|_1\|Q\|_1\|\widetilde A\|_1
\leq1.
\]
Every eigenvalue $\zeta$ of $WQ\widetilde A$ therefore
satisfies $|\zeta|\leq1$. Since
$H=WQ\widetilde A-I$ is invertible, $\zeta\ne1$,
and consequently $\operatorname{Re}(\zeta-1)<0$.
Thus all eigenvalues of $H$ have strictly negative
real parts. The associated ODE
\[
\dot z=zH+C
\]
has the unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium
$-CH^{-1}$. In \eqref{eq:main_recur_vec}, the state
variables and martingale differences are bounded,
the step sizes are $1/(t+1)$, and the remainder tends
to zero almost surely. Lemma~\ref{lem:sas} therefore
gives the claimed convergence.
The same argument applies when the recursion is
initialized at any fixed finite time.

name: Invertibility via mixed sampling or subcritical reinforcement

label: eq:nullvector
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $H$ is singular. Since $H$ is a real matrix, there exists a nonzero real row vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N) $  such that $vH=0$, i.e. $v=vWQ\widetilde A.$ Hence, for each $k\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}$, 
    \begin{equation} \label{eq:nullvector} 
    v_k = \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} (2q_r-1)\mu_{rk} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{jr}v_j . 
    \end{equation} 
    Choose $l\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}$ such that $|v_l|=\max_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}|v_i|,$ and define $\widetilde v=\frac{v}{|v_l|}.$ Then 
    \[ |\widetilde v_l|=1, \qquad |\widetilde v_i|\le 1, \quad i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$} . \]
    Applying \eqref{eq:nullvector} with $k=l$ gives
    \[ 1 = |\widetilde v_l| = \left| \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} (2q_r-1)\mu_{rl} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{jr}\widetilde v_j \right|. \]
    Using the triangle inequality, $1 \le \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} |2q_r-1|\,|\mu_{rl}| \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{jr}|\widetilde v_j|.$
    Since $W$ is column-stochastic and $|\widetilde v_j|\le 1$ for all $j$, 
    \[ 1 \le \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} |2q_r-1|\,|\mu_{rl}| \le \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}|\mu_{rl}| \le 1, 
    \] where the last inequality follows from \eqref{reinforcement_assumption}. Therefore equality must hold throughout. Consequently,
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item every in-neighbour $r$ of $l$ satisfies $|2q_r-1|=1$, i.e. $r$ is not mixed-sampling;
    \item the vertex $l$ is critical, i.e. $\sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}|\mu_{rl}|=1$; 
    \item $\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{jr}|\widetilde v_j|=1$ for every $r\to l$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    Since the weights in each column of $W$ are nonnegative and sum to one, the third condition implies that $|\widetilde v_j|=1$ for every $j$ with $w_{jr}>0$ and every $r\to l$. Hence 
    \[ |\widetilde v_j|=1, \qquad j\in N_l^{(2)}. \]
    Repeating the same argument at any vertex $x$ satisfying $|\widetilde v_x|=1$, we obtain inductively that 
    \[ |\widetilde v_j|=1, \qquad j\in N_l^{(2m)}, \quad m\ge 1. \]
    Moreover, for every $m\ge0$, 
    \begin{itemize} 
    \item every vertex in $N_l^{(2m+1)}$ is not \textit{mixed-sampling},
    \item every vertex in $N_l^{(2m)}$ is \textit{critical}.
    \end{itemize}
    Thus, the existence of a nonzero null vector forces all vertices in odd layers to satisfy $q_j\in\{0,1\}$ and all vertices in even layers to be critical.

    We now derive a contradiction. Suppose condition {\rm (i)} holds. First assume that $\mathcal G$ contains an odd cycle and that there exists a vertex $r^*$ with $|2q_{r^*}-1|<1$.  Since $\mathcal G$ is strongly connected, there exists a directed path from $r^*$ to $l$. Combining this path with the odd cycle, if necessary, yields a directed path from $r^*$ to $l$ of odd length. Hence $r^*\in N_l^{(2m+1)}$ for some $m\ge0$, contradicting the fact that every vertex in an odd layer must satisfy $|2q_j-1|=1$.

    Now, suppose there exist two mixed-sampling vertices $r^*$ and $r'$ connected by a directed path of odd length, i.e.  $r^*\rightsquigarrow r'$ (or $r'\rightsquigarrow r^*$) via a path of odd length. Then relative to $l$, at least one of the vertices $r^*$ and $r'$ must belong to an odd layer, giving the same contradiction. 

Next assume that condition {\rm (ii)} holds. The argument is analogous. If $\mathcal G$ contains an odd cycle and there exists a subcritical vertex $v$, then there exists an even-length directed walk from $v$ to $l$. Thus $v\in N_l^{(2m)}$ for some $m\ge0$, contradicting the fact that every even-layer vertex is critical.
    
Similarly, if two subcritical vertices are connected by a directed path of odd length, then relative to $l$ at least one of them must belong to an even layer, again contradicting the requirement that every even-layer vertex be critical.  Therefore $H$ is invertible. The convergence statement follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:deterministic_limit}.

label: thm:GPA
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:GPA}
Suppose that $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ contains an odd cycle.
Assume further that all vertices are positive-critical
and that $q_v\in\{0,1\}$ for every $v\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}$.
Then $WQ\widetilde A-I$ is invertible if and only if
$\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ does not admit a partition under the GPA.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All vertices are positive-critical and all nodes are either preferential or de-preferential, 
                                                                                                     
we have $\sum_{j\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}\mu_{jr}=1$  and $2q_r-1\in\{-1,1\}$ for each $r \in [N]$. First suppose that $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ admits a partition under the GPA. Define a sign vector
$\sigma=(\sigma_i)_{i\in[N]}$ by
\[
\sigma_i=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } i\in P_1\cup D_2,\\
-1, & \text{if } i\in P_2\cup D_1.
\end{cases}
\]

The pattern of the GPA partition shown in Figure~\ref{fig:gpa_partition}
implies that for every directed two-step path $i\to r\to k$,
$\sigma_k=(2q_i-1)\sigma_i$. Indeed, if $i\in\mbox{${\mathcal P}$}$, then $2q_i-1=1$, and the GPA places $i$ and $k$ in
classes carrying the same  sign. If $i\in\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}$, then $2q_i-1=-1$,
and the GPA places $i$ and $k$ in classes carrying opposite  signs. Using this, we get that for every $k\in[N]$,
\begin{eqnarray*} (\sigma Q\widetilde A W)_k &=& \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} w_{rk} \sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}(2q_i-1)\mu_{ir}\sigma_i= \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} w_{rk} \sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}\mu_{ir}\sigma_k\\ &=& \sigma_k\sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} w_{rk} \sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}\mu_{ir}= \sigma_k. 
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent 
Thus, $\sigma Q\widetilde A W=\sigma$. Set $v=\sigma Q\widetilde A$. Then
$v\neq0$, since $vW=\sigma Q\widetilde A W=\sigma\neq0$. Moreover, $vWQ\widetilde A
=
\sigma Q\widetilde A WQ\widetilde A
=
\sigma Q\widetilde A
=
v$.
Therefore $v(WQ\widetilde A-I)=0$, and so $WQ\widetilde A-I$ is singular.

To prove the converse, now suppose that $WQ\widetilde A-I$ is singular. Since this is a real matrix, there exists a non-zero real row vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)$
such that $v(WQ\widetilde A-I)=0$. Let $u=vW$. Then $u\neq0$, because otherwise
$v=vWQ\widetilde A=0$, which contradicts the choice of $v$. Also,
$uQ\widetilde A W
=
vWQ\widetilde A W
=
vW
=
u$.

Choose $l\in[N]$ such that $|u_l|=\max_{i\in[N]}|u_i|$, and normalize so that
$|u_l|=1$. Then $|u_i|\leq1$ for all $i\in[N]$. From $uQ\widetilde A W=u$,
the $k$-th coordinate satisfies
\[
u_k = \sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{rk}
\sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}(2q_i-1)\mu_{ir}u_i.
\]
Now, by the triangle inequality,
\begin{align*}
|u_k|
=
\left|
\sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{rk}
\sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}(2q_i-1)\mu_{ir}u_i
\right| &\leq
\sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{rk}
\sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}\mu_{ir}|2q_i-1|\,|u_i|\\
&\leq
\sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{rk}
\sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}\mu_{ir} =1.
\end{align*}
Now suppose that $|u_k|=1$. Since the coefficients
$w_{rk}\mu_{ir}$ are non-negative and 
$\sum_{r\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{rk}
\sum_{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}\mu_{ir} = 1,$
we have that, for every directed two-step path $i\to r\to k$, $|u_i|=1$, and all the terms $(2q_i-1)u_i$ have the same sign as $u_k$. Therefore, $(2q_i-1)u_i=u_k$ for every directed two-step path $i\to r\to k$.


Starting from $l$ and repeating this argument along two-step paths, we get
$|u_i|=1$ for every vertex reached by the two-step exploration from $l$. Since
$\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ is strongly connected and contains an odd cycle, this two-step
exploration reaches every vertex. Therefore $u_i\in\{-1,1\}$ for every
$i\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}$. Moreover, for every directed two-step path $i\to r\to k$, $u_k=(2q_i-1)u_i$. Multiplying $u$ by $-1$ if necessary, we may assume that $u_l=1$ when
$l\in\mbox{${\mathcal P}$}$ and $u_l=-1$ when $l\in\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}$. Define
\[
P_1=\{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal P}$}:u_i=1\},\qquad
P_2=\{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal P}$}:u_i=-1\},
\]
and
\[
D_1=\{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}:u_i=-1\},\qquad
D_2=\{i\in\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}:u_i=1\}.
\]
These four sets are mutually disjoint and their union is $\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}$. We claim that the GPA, started from $l$, assigns vertices consistent with these
four sets. This is proved by induction over the steps of the algorithm. The
initial assignment is consistent by our choice of the sign of $u_l$. Suppose
that all vertices assigned up to some stage agree with the four sets above.
If the algorithm uses a directed two-step path $i\to r\to k$ to assign a new
vertex $i$ from an already assigned vertex $k$, then $u_k=(2q_i-1)u_i$. Hence the new assignment also agrees with the four sets above. Therefore GPA never
assigns a vertex to two incompatible classes. Since the two-step exploration
reaches every vertex, $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ admits a partition under the GPA. 

We have shown that $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ admits a partition under the GPA if and only if
$WQ\widetilde A-I$ is singular. Equivalently, $WQ\widetilde A-I$ is
invertible if and only if $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ does not admit a partition under GPA.

label: prop:evencycle
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:evencycle}
Suppose $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ is a directed even cycle of length $2k$,
with $\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}_1$ and $\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}_2$ as defined above.
Suppose that, for some $a\in\{1,2\}$, every vertex in
$\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}_a$ is positive-critical, while every vertex in
$\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}_{3-a}$ is either preferential or de-preferential.
If $|\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}\cap\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}_{3-a}|$ is even, then
$WQ\widetilde A-I$ is singular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to consider $a=1$; the other case follows
by shifting the cyclic labelling by one vertex.
Since every odd-labelled vertex is positive-critical
and has exactly one reinforcement in-neighbour,
$\mu_{2j,2j+1}=1$ for $j=1,\ldots,k$, with indices
read modulo $2k$. Moreover,
$\prod_{j=1}^{k}(2q_{2j}-1)
=(-1)^{\left|\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}\cap\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}_2 \right|}=1.$
The determinant factors as
\[
\det(WQ\widetilde A-I)
=
\left(1-\prod_{j=1}^{k}
(2q_{2j-1}-1)\mu_{2j-1,2j}\right) \times
\left(1-\prod_{j=1}^{k}
(2q_{2j}-1)\mu_{2j,2j+1}\right).
\]
The second factor is zero, proving the assertion.

label: rem:Weak
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:Weak}
The results in this section can be extended from strongly
connected graphs to weakly connected graphs. We briefly indicate the extension.
\begin{itemize}
    \item Suppose first that there is a non-empty set of {\it stubborn nodes}
    $\mathcal S\subseteq \mathcal V$, where a node $i\in\mathcal S$ is called
    stubborn if $d_i^{\mathrm{in}}=0$. If $S \neq \emptyset$ and the subgraph induced by
    $\mathcal V\setminus \mathcal S$ is strongly connected, then the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:deterministic_limit} continues to hold with the limit on $V \setminus S$ having the form different from equation\eqref{deter_limit}. The configurations of the nodes in $S$ remain unchanged over time. 

                                                   

    \item Suppose next that there are no stubborn nodes, but the graph is
    still weakly connected. Decompose $\mathcal G$ into its strongly connected
    components. Using an argument similar to Corollary~1 of \cite{kaur2025interacting}, it
    is enough to check the deterministic-limit condition on the stubborn
    strongly connected components. Here, a stubborn strongly connected
    component is a strongly connected subgraph induced by a set
    $F\subseteq\mathcal V$ such that there is no $j\notin F$, $v\in F$
    with $j\to v$.
\end{itemize}

label: lem:commute
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:commute}
Assume {\rm \bf(B)} and {\rm \bf(C)} hold. Then $\tilde J$ commutes with $Q\widetilde A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $U\in\mathcal B$, let
$\sigma_U=\begin{cases}1,& U=P_1\text{ or }P_2,\\ -1,& U=D_1\text{ or }D_2.\end{cases}$
Since $\mathbf{1}_UQ=\sigma_U\mathbf{1}_U$,  {\rm \bf (C)} gives 
$\mathbf{1}_UQ\widetilde{A}=\sigma_U\mathbf{1}_U\widetilde{A}
=\sigma_U\sum_{V\in\mathcal B}\mu_{UV}\mathbf{1}_V$. Recall that
$\tilde J=\sum_{U\in\mathcal B}|U|^{-1}\mathbf{1}_U^\top\mathbf{1}_U$. Hence,
\[
\tilde JQ\widetilde{A}
=
\sum_{U,V\in\mathcal B}
\frac{\sigma_U \mu_{UV}}{|U|}\mathbf{1}_U^\top\mathbf{1}_V.
\]
Next, we compute $Q \widetilde{A} \tilde J$. Since
$\tilde J=\sum_{V\in\mathcal B}|V|^{-1}\mathbf{1}_V^\top\mathbf{1}_V$, we have
\[
Q \widetilde{A} \tilde J
=
\sum_{V\in\mathcal B}
\frac{1}{|V|}
(Q \widetilde{A} \mathbf{1}_V^\top)\mathbf{1}_V.
\]
For $i\in U$, the $i$-th entry of $Q \widetilde{A} \mathbf{1}_V^\top$ equals
$\sigma_U \sum_{\substack{j:\,i\to j\\ j\in V}}\mu_{ij}$. By {\rm \bf (B)} and the GPA block structure,
$\sum_{\substack{j:\,i\to j\\ j\in V}}\mu_{ij}$ is constant over $i\in U$; denote this constant by
$r_{UV}$. Therefore
\[
Q \widetilde{A} \tilde J
=
\sum_{U,V\in\mathcal B}
\frac{\sigma_Ur_{UV}}{|V|}\mathbf{1}_U^\top\mathbf{1}_V.
\]
It remains to compare the constants in the two expressions. The total mass in
the $U,V$ block of $\widetilde A$ is $\sum\limits_{\substack{i\in U,\ j\in V\\ i\to j}}\mu_{ij}$. By {\rm \bf (C)}, each column in $V$ receives weight $\mu_{UV}$ from rows in $U$, so
this total is $|V|\mu_{UV}$. By the definition of $r_{UV}$, each row in $U$
sends weight $r_{UV}$ to columns in $V$, so the same total is
$|U|r_{UV}$. Hence $|V|\mu_{UV}=|U|r_{UV}$, or equivalently
$\mu_{UV}/|U|=r_{UV}/|V|$. The two displayed expressions are therefore equal, and
so $\tilde JQ\widetilde{A}=Q \widetilde{A} \tilde J$.

name: Almost Sure Convergence of $\Z_t$

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Phi_t=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)$. We first apply Proposition~\ref{prop:Var} with $U=I-\tilde J$. Its assumptions are satisfied because $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}$ is constant on the four parts of the partition by (C), so $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}(I-\tilde J)=0$; $\tilde J$ commutes with $Q\widetilde{A}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:commute}, so $Q\widetilde{A}(I-\tilde J)=(I-\tilde J)Q\widetilde{A}$; and $\hat v$ is constant on the four parts of the partition, so $\hat v(I-\tilde J)=0$. Hence Proposition~\ref{prop:Var} gives $\Phi_t\to{\bf 0}$ in $\mathcal L^2$.

On the other hand, by Theorem~\ref{thm:QM1}, $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$ has an almost sure limit; denote it by $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}^*$. Therefore $\Phi_t=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)$ converges almost surely to $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}^*(I-\tilde J)$. Since $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$ is bounded, $\|\Phi_t\|^2$ is bounded, and bounded convergence together with $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\Phi_t\|^2]\to0$ gives $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}^*(I-\tilde J)\|^2]=0$. Thus $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}^*(I-\tilde J)={\bf 0}$ almost surely, and consequently $\Phi_t\to{\bf 0}$ almost surely. This proves that $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde{J})\to0$ almost surely.

label: eq:projected_recursion
title: Proof
body_md:
Multiplying \eqref{eq:centered_SA_recursion} on the right by $U$ gives
\[
        Y_{t+1}
        =
        Y_t\left(I+\frac{\Lambda-I}{t+1}\right)
        +
        \frac{1}{t+1}\left(\Delta M_{t+1}U+\epsilon_{t+1}U\right).
\]
Hence, for each \(r\in[N]\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projected_recursion}
        Y_{t+1}(r)
        =
        \left(1+\frac{\lambda_r'}{t+1}\right)Y_t(r)
        +
        \frac{(\Delta M_{t+1}U)(r)+(\epsilon_{t+1}U)(r)}{t+1}.
\end{equation}

Choose a fixed integer $t_0$ sufficiently large so that
$1+\lambda_r'/k\ne 0$ for all $k\ge t_0+1$ and all $r$. This avoids possible zero factors in the Euler products. Put \(d_{t_0}(r)=1\)
and, for \(t\geq t_0+1\),
\(d_t(r):=\prod_{j=t_0+1}^{t}(1+\lambda_r'/j)\). By the gamma-function asymptotic,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dt_asymp_projected}
        d_t(r)
        =
        \frac{\Gamma(t+1+\lambda_r')\Gamma(t_0+1)}
             {\Gamma(t_0+1+\lambda_r')\Gamma(t+1)}
        \asymp
        t^{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')}.\end{equation}
Iterating \eqref{eq:projected_recursion} gives the following.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projected_variation_constants}
        Y_t(r)
        =
        d_t(r)
        \left(
            Y_{t_0}(r)
            +
            \mathcal L_t(r)
        \right)
        +
        \mathcal E_t(r),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal L_t(r)
        :=
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t-1}
        \frac{(\Delta M_{k+1}U)(r)}
             {(k+1)d_{k+1}(r)}$
and
        $\mathcal E_t(r)
        :=
        d_t(r)
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t-1}
        \frac{(\epsilon_{k+1}U)(r)}
             {(k+1)d_{k+1}(r)}$.  We analyse separately the martingale term $\mathcal L_t(r)$ and the accumulated error term $\mathcal E_t(r)$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[Step 1:] Since the martingale difference $\Delta M_t$ is  bounded and $U$ is fixed,
there is a deterministic constant $K>0$ such that $| (\Delta M_t U)(r)|\le K$ for all $t,r$. Hence the predictable quadratic variation of $\mathcal L_t(r)$ satisfies
\[
        \big\langle \mathcal L(r)\big\rangle_t
        :=
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t-1}
        \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\left[
        \left.
        \left|
        \frac{(\Delta M_{k+1} U)(r)}
             {(k+1)d_{k+1}(r)}
        \right|^2
        \right|\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_k
        \right]
        \le
        K^2\,\ell_t(r),
\]
where
$\ell_t(r)
        :=
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t-1}
        \left|(k+1)d_{k+1}(r)\right|^{-2}.$ Using \eqref{eq:dt_asymp_projected}, we immediately get that $\ell_t(r)  \asymp  \sum_{k=t_0}^{t}  k^{-2-2\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')}$. Therefore
\[
\ell_t(r)
=
\begin{cases}
O\!\left(t^{-1-2\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')}\right),
& \mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')<-1/2,\\[6pt]
O(\log t),
& \mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')=-1/2,
\end{cases}
\]
and $\ell_t(r) \to \ell_\infty(r) \coloneqq \sum_{k=t_0}^{\infty}  \left|(k+1)d_{k+1}(r)\right|^{-2} < \infty$  for $\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')>-1/2$.



We now apply Theorem~\ref{aux:duflo_martingale_estimate} separately to the
real and imaginary parts of the complex martingale \(\mathcal L_t(r)\).
Since \(\langle \mathcal L(r)\rangle_t\le K^2\ell_t(r)\), it follows
that, whenever \(\ell_t(r)\to\infty\), for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:L_bound_by_ell}
        \mathcal L_t(r)
        =
        o\!\left(
        (\ell_t(r))^{1/2}
        (\log \ell_t(r))^{1/2+\varepsilon}
        \right)
        \qquad\text{a.s.}
\end{equation}
If \(\ell_t(r)\) converges, then the same theorem gives $\mathcal L_t(r)
        \xrightarrow{a.s.}
        \mathcal L_\infty(r)$, where \(\mathcal L_\infty(r)\) is finite almost surely. In particular, this
convergence holds when \(\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')>-1/2\).

Multiplying \eqref{eq:L_bound_by_ell} by $d_t(r)$ gives, in the diffusive and critical cases,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dL_rates}
        d_t(r)\mathcal L_t(r)
        =
        \begin{cases}
        o\!\left(
        t^{-1/2}(\log t)^{1/2+\varepsilon}
        \right),
        & \mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')<-1/2,\\[8pt]
        o\!\left(
        t^{-1/2}
        (\log t)^{1/2}
        (\log\log t)^{1/2+\varepsilon}
        \right),
        & \mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')=-1/2,
        \end{cases}
        \qquad\text{a.s.}
\end{equation}



\item[Step 2:]



We now estimate the accumulated error
$\mathcal E_t(r)$ using \eqref{eq:error_one_step_bound}.
Since $\|\epsilon_{k+1}\|=O((k+1)^{-1})$ almost surely and
$|d_t(r)|\asymp t^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}$,
there exists an almost surely finite random constant $K>0$,
independent of $t$, such that
\[
        |\mathcal E_t(r)|
        \le
        K |d_t(r)|
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t-1}
        \frac{1}{(k+1)^2 |d_{k+1}(r)|}
        \le
        K t^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t}
        k^{-2-\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}.
\]


It follows that
\begin{equation} \label{eq:errordecay}
        |\mathcal E_t(r)|
        =
        \begin{cases}
        O(t^{-1}),
        & \mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')<-1,\\[6pt]
        O((\log t)/t),
        & \mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')=-1,\\[6pt]
        O(t^{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r')}),
        & -1<\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r').
        \end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}
In particular, for $\mathrm{Re}(\lambda_r') \le -1/2$ this error is negligible when compared with the corresponding martingale rate in \eqref{eq:dL_rates}. Using the estimates from \eqref{eq:dL_rates}  in \eqref{eq:projected_variation_constants} (combined with the fact that the term $d_t(r)Y_{t_0}(r)$ is negligible compared with the
corresponding bound in \eqref{eq:dL_rates})  proves the diffusive and critical assertions.

\noindent In the superdiffusive case, \(-1/2<\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')<0\). So, 
\(2+\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')>1\). We therefore have $
        |\mathcal E_t(r)|
        =
        O\!\left(t^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}\right)
        \text{a.s.}$
Further, 
\[
        \frac{Y_t(r)}{d_t(r)}
        =
        Y_{t_0}(r)
        +\mathcal L_t(r)
        +
        \sum_{k=t_0}^{t-1}
        \frac{(\epsilon_{k+1}U)(r)}
             {(k+1)d_{k+1}(r)}.
\]
 Recall that in this regime, $\mathcal L_t(r)
        \xrightarrow{a.s.}
        \mathcal L_\infty(r)$, where \(\mathcal L_\infty(r)\) is finite almost surely. Using
\(\|\epsilon_{k+1}\|=O((k+1)^{-1})\) and
\(|d_k(r)|\asymp k^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}\), we get that the last series
converges absolutely. Therefore
\(Y_t(r)/d_t(r)\) converges almost surely to a finite random variable. Again using \(|d_t(r)|\asymp t^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}\), we obtain
$Y_t(r)
        =
        O\!\left(t^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_r')}\right)
        \text{a.s.}$ This proves the assertion in the superdiffusive regime.



\noindent Finally, since \(U\) is invertible and \(X_t=Y_tU^{-1}\), there exists a
constant \(K_U>0\) such that $\|X_t\|\le K_U\|Y_t\|$.
Thus the coordinatewise projected bounds imply the asserted bounds for $\|X_t\|=\|\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t-\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*\|$. This completes the proof.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:limiting_martingale_covariance}
Assume that $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\to\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*$ almost surely, where $\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*$
may be random. Let $\Delta M_{t+1}$ be the martingale
difference appearing in \eqref{eq:main_recur_vec}. Then
\[
        \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\!\left[
        (\Delta M_{t+1})^\top \Delta M_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t
        \right]
        \xrightarrow{a.s.}
        \widetilde A^\top \Gamma'\widetilde A,
\]
where \(\Gamma'\) is a diagonal matrix with entries
$\Gamma'_{jj}=p_j^\star(1-p_j^\star)$, $p_j^\star=q_js_j^\star+(1-q_j)(1-s_j^\star)$ and 
        $s_j^\star
        =\sum_{k\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{kj}\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*(k)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $j$, set $ s_j(t):=\sum_{k\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{kj}Z_t(k)$ and $p_j(t) \coloneqq q_j s_j(t)+(1-q_j)(1-s_j(t)) = (2q_j-1)s_j(t)+(1-q_j)$. Then, conditionally on $\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t$, the sampling indicator $\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j)$ is Bernoulli with parameter $p_j(t)$. 

Define the row vector $\Delta M'_{t+1}
        :=
        \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}
        -
        \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]$.
Then $\Delta M_{t+1}=\Delta M'_{t+1}\widetilde A$.  By conditional independence of the draws at a fixed time, \(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\!\left[
        (\Delta M'_{t+1})^\top \Delta M'_{t+1}
        \mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t
        \right]\) is
diagonal. Its \(j\)-th diagonal entry is 
        $p_j(t)(1-p_j(t))$. 
        
Since \(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\to\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*\) almost surely, we have  $s_j(t)\xrightarrow{a.s.}s_j^\star
        :=
        \sum_{k\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{kj}\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*(k)$. Hence $p_j(t)\xrightarrow{a.s.}p_j^\star
        :=
        q_js_j^\star+(1-q_j)(1-s_j^\star)$, and therefore
 $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\!\left[
        (\Delta M'_{t+1})^\top \Delta M'_{t+1}
        \mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t
        \right]
        \xrightarrow{a.s.}
        \Gamma' $, where \(\Gamma'\) is the diagonal matrix defined in the statement of the
lemma. Finally, since \(\Delta M_{t+1}=\Delta M'_{t+1}\widetilde A\),
\[
        \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\!\left[
        (\Delta M_{t+1})^\top \Delta M_{t+1}
        \mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t
        \right]
        \xrightarrow{a.s.}
        \widetilde A^\top \Gamma'\widetilde A.
\]
This proves the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
We verify the assumptions of the stochastic-approximation compact LIL
stated in Theorem~\ref{aux:MP_compact_LIL} for the centred recursion
\eqref{eq:centered_SA_recursion}. This verification follows
\cite[Theorem~11]{das2024elephant}, with the remainder controlled
by \eqref{eq:error_one_step_bound}.
We use Theorem~\ref{aux:MP_compact_LIL} for the stochastic
approximation algorithm
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SA_LIL}
        X_{t+1}
        =
        X_t+\gamma_t\big[h(X_t)+r_{t+1}\big]
        +\sigma_t\xi_{t+1},
\end{equation}
with $h(x)=xH=x(B-I), r_{t+1}=\epsilon_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}=\Delta M_{t+1}$
and $\gamma_t=\sigma_t=\frac{1}{t+1}$. Thus, 
\[
        v_t:=\frac{\gamma_t}{\sigma_t^2}=t+1,
        \qquad
        s_t:=\sum_{k=1}^{t}\gamma_k
        =
        \sum_{k=1}^{t}\frac1{k+1}
        \sim \log t.
\]
We now check assumptions {\bf (1)--(5)} of Theorem~\ref{aux:MP_compact_LIL}.

\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{(1)}
Under the deterministic-limit assumption of the theorem, $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mbox{${\mathbf Z}$}^*$. Therefore, $X_t\xrightarrow{a.s.}0$. Thus the stochastic approximation algorithm in \eqref{eq:SA_LIL} is consistent, with equilibrium $0$.

\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{(2)}
The function $h(x)=xH$ is linear, so its Jacobian at $0$
is $H=B-I$. Set $L:=1-\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_1)$.
Then
\[
\max_{\mu\in\mathrm{Sp}(H)}\operatorname{Re}(\mu)
=\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_1)-1=-L.
\]
Since $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_1)<1/2$, we have
$L>1/2$. Therefore the linear drift is attractive.

\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{(3)}
We clearly have  $\gamma_t\to0, \sigma_t\to0,
        s_t\to\infty$ and
        $\frac{\gamma_t}{\gamma_{t+1}}=1+O(\gamma_t)$. Moreover,
\[
        \frac1{\gamma_t}
        \left(
        1-\frac{v_{t-1}}{v_t}
        \right)
        =
        (t+1)\left(1-\frac{t}{t+1}\right)
        =
        1.
\]
Thus the parameter $\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}$ in
Theorem~\ref{aux:MP_compact_LIL} equals $1$. Since $L>1/2$, we have $1\in(0,2L)$, so {\bf (3)} holds.

\smallskip

\noindent
\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{(4)}
The martingale
difference term in \eqref{eq:SA_LIL} has uniformly bounded increments. Hence, for every $\delta>0$, $\sup_{t\ge0} \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\!\left[\|\Delta M_{t+1}\|^{2+\delta} \mid \mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t \right] <\infty$ a.s. Therefore, by the sufficient martingale-difference condition for {\bf (4)} stated
in Comment~(4) preceding Theorem~1 of Mokkadem and Pelletier
\cite[Comment~(4)]{MP2005}, the required almost sure invariance principle
holds with covariance matrix $\Gamma$. Thus {\bf (4)} holds.

\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{(5)} Using \eqref{eq:error_one_step_bound}, we have  $\|\epsilon_{t+1}\|= O(v_t^{-1/2})$ a.s. Thus {\bf (5)} holds by taking $r_{t+1}^{(1)}=\epsilon_{t+1}$ and the remaining
$o(\|X_t\|)$ term equal to zero.

\smallskip

\noindent All assumptions of Theorem~\ref{aux:MP_compact_LIL} are now verified. Therefore
\(\{\sqrt{v_t/(2\log s_t)}\,X_t\}_{t\ge1}\) is relatively compact almost surely,
and its limit set is the ellipsoid associated with
\[
        \int_0^\infty
        \exp\!\left((H+\tfrac12 I)^\top u\right)
        \Gamma
        \exp\!\left((H+\tfrac12 I)u\right)
        \,du .
\]
Since \(H=B-I\), the above matrix is precisely \(\Sigma_\infty\) defined in
\eqref{eq:Sigma_infty_LIL}. Also, \(v_t=t+1\) and \(s_t\sim\log t\), so the
normalization \(\sqrt{v_t/(2\log s_t)}\) is asymptotic to
\(\sqrt{t/(2\log\log t)}\). This proves the theorem.

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply Zhang's stochastic approximation CLT
\cite[Theorem~2.3]{MR3582813} to the centred recursion \eqref{eq:centered_SA_recursion}. In Zhang's notation, the drift is
\(h(x)=x(I-B)\), and hence the eigenvalues of \(Dh(0)\) are
\(1-\lambda_r\), \(1\le r\le N\). Therefore
\[
        \min_{1\le r\le N}\operatorname{Re}(1-\lambda_r)
        =
        1-\operatorname{Re}(\lambda_1)        >
        \frac12 .
\]
The deterministic-limit assumption gives \(X_t\to0\) almost surely. The
martingale difference term has uniformly bounded increments, so the required
Lindeberg condition holds. Moreover, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:limiting_martingale_covariance}, its conditional covariance
converges almost surely to \(\Gamma\). Finally, by
\eqref{eq:error_one_step_bound},
\[
        \sum_{k=1}^{t}\epsilon_k
        =
        O(\log t)
        =
        o(\sqrt t)
        \qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Thus all assumptions of \cite[Theorem~2.3]{MR3582813} are satisfied, and the
conclusion follows. The covariance matrix appearing in that theorem
is exactly $\Sigma_\infty$, since
$-(Dh(0)-\tfrac12 I)=B-\tfrac12 I$. This proves the theorem.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since every vertex is positive-critical, $\mathbf{1} \widetilde A=\mathbf{1}$. 
Multiplying the identity \[ \widetilde A\mathbf{1}^{\top} = (\mu_{\mathcal P}^{out} +\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out}) \mathbf{1}^{\top} \] from the left by $\mathbf{1}$ gives 
 \[ N = \mathbf{1}\widetilde A\mathbf{1}^{\top} = (\mu_{\mathcal P}^{out} +\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out}) \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} = N(\mu_{\mathcal P}^{out} +\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out}). \] 
 Hence \[ \mu_{\mathcal P}^{out} +\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out} =1. \]
 Since $\mathbf{1}  = \mathbf{1}_{\mbox{${\mathcal P}$}} + \mathbf{1}_{\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}}$ we get 
 \[\mbox{$\widetilde{A}$} \mathbf{1}^\top  = \mu^{out}_{\mbox{${\mathcal P}$}}\mathbf{1}^{\top} + \mu^{out}_{\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}}\mathbf{1}^{\top} = \mathbf{1}^\top.\]
             
                                              
                                 
                                                                                                                                
                                               
             
                
                                                                              
Now let $S=\mathbf{1}_{P_1}^{\top}+\mathbf{1}_{D_2}^{\top}
 -\mathbf{1}_{P_2}^{\top}-\mathbf{1}_{D_1}^{\top}$. Then
 $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tS=Z_t^{P_1}+Z_t^{D_2}-Z_t^{P_2}-Z_t^{D_1}$.
 From \ref{eq:main_recur_vec} and {\rm \bf (A2)} we get, 
 \begin{eqnarray}\label{gen_exp}
 \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}S\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
 &=&
 \mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tS\left(1-\frac{1}{t+1}\right)
 +
 \frac{1}{t+1}
 \left( \mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tQ\widetilde A+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A\right)S\\
 &=&
 \mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tS+
 \frac{1}{t+1}
 \left[
 \mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(Q\widetilde A-I)S+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde AS
 \right].
 \end{eqnarray}
 Therefore, it is enough to show that $(Q\widetilde A-I)S=\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde AS=\mathbf{0}$. Using the structure of the adjacency matrix (from \eqref{adjacency-partition}) we get 
 \[ \widetilde AS = \mathbf{1}_{P_1}^{\top} -\mathbf{1}_{D_2}^{\top} -\mathbf{1}_{P_2}^{\top} +\mathbf{1}_{D_1}^{\top}  \]
 and
 \[ Q\widetilde AS = \mathbf{1}_{P_1}^{\top}  +\mathbf{1}_{D_2}^{\top}-\mathbf{1}_{P_2}^{\top} -\mathbf{1}_{D_1}^{\top} = S. \]
 Similarly, we get $\mathbf{1}_{\mbox{${\mathcal D}$}} \mbox{$\widetilde{A}$} S = \mathbf{0}$ when $d_1 = d_2$.

label: eq:EVar
title: Proof
body_md:
Writing \eqref{noderecurnew} in vector form, we get

\begin{align}\label{eq:EVar}
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
&=
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\left(1-\frac{1}{t+1}\right)
+\frac{(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tQ+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D})\widetilde A}{t+1}
\nonumber\\
&=
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tK_t+\frac{\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A}{t+1}.
\end{align}
where $K_t:=I-\frac{1}{t+1}\left(I-Q\widetilde{A}\right)$. Let $D_t:=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tU$. Since $Q\widetilde{A}U=UQ\widetilde{A}$, we have $K_tU=UK_t$. Further, since $\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}U=0$, we get $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_{t+1}\mid \mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tK_tU=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tUK_t=D_tK_t$. Taking expectation and iterating gives
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_{t+1}]=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\prod_{i=0}^{t}K_i U.
\]
Using {\rm \bf (D)}, write
$I-Q\widetilde{A}=P\Lambda P^{-1}$, where
$\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_N)$. Then, $$\prod_{i=0}^{t}K_i
=
P\prod_{i=0}^{t}
\left(I-\frac{1}{i+1}\Lambda\right)P^{-1}.$$ Since $Q$ only changes signs of rows and the column sums of $\widetilde{A}$ are $1$, every eigenvalue $\eta$ of $Q\widetilde{A}$ satisfies $|\eta|\leq 1$. Hence every eigenvalue $\nu=1-\eta$ of $I-Q\widetilde{A}$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}(\nu)\geq 0$. Let $s$ be such that $\nu_s=0$, and let $e_s$ denote the $s$-th standard row vector. Then,
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{t}
\left(I-\frac{1}{i+1}\Lambda\right)
\longrightarrow e_s^\top e_s.
\]
Moreover, for every $\nu_i\neq 0$,
\[
\prod_{j=0}^{t}
\left|1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_i\right|
=
\mathcal{O}\left(t^{-\operatorname{Re}(\nu_i)}\right).
\]
Since the $s$-th row of $P^{-1}$ is a left eigenvector
corresponding to the eigenvalue $0$, it is a multiple of
$\hat v$. Hence $\hat vU=0$ gives $e_sP^{-1}U=0$. Therefore,
$\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_t]=\mathcal{O}\left(t^{-\nu^*}\right)$. Now, since
$\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}
=
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\left(1-\frac{1}{t+1}\right)
+
\frac{\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}\widetilde{A}}{t+1}$,
we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1})
&=&
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid \mathcal F_t)]
+
\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid \mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t])
\\
&=&
\frac{\widetilde{A}^\top}{(t+1)^2}
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}\mid \mathcal F_t)]\widetilde{A}
+
K_t^\top\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t)K_t.
\end{eqnarray*}
Define $N_t:=\widetilde{A}^\top \ \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}\mid \mathcal F_t)]\widetilde{A}$. The entries of $N_t$ are uniformly bounded. Thus
\begin{eqnarray*}\label{Var_decay2}
\operatorname{Var}(D_{t+1})
&=&
U^\top\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1})U
\\
&=&
U^\top
\left[
\sum_{k=0}^{t}
\frac{1}{(k+1)^2}
\left(\prod_{i=0}^{t-k-1}K_{t-i}^\top\right)
N_k
\left(\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}K_i\right)
\right]
U
\\
&=&
U^\top(P^{-1})^\top\Delta_tP^{-1}U,
\end{eqnarray*}
where
\[
\Delta_t:=
\sum_{k=0}^{t}
\frac{1}{(k+1)^2}
\left[
\prod_{i=0}^{t-k-1}
\left(I-\frac{1}{t-i+1}\Lambda\right)
\right]
P^\top N_kP
\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}
\left(I-\frac{1}{i+1}\Lambda\right).
\]
Let $\beta_k(p,q)$ be the $(p,q)$-th entry of $P^\top N_kP$. Since the entries of $N_k$ are uniformly bounded, so are the $\beta_k(p,q)$'s. The $(p,q)$-th entry of $\Delta_t$ is
\[
\Delta_t(p,q)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{t}
\frac{1}{(k+1)^2}
\left[
\prod_{i=0}^{t-k-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{t-i+1}\nu_p\right)
\right]
\beta_k(p,q)
\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}
\left(1-\frac{1}{i+1}\nu_q\right).
\]
Using Euler's approximation for $(p,q)\neq(s,s)$, there is a constant $C'$ such that
\begin{eqnarray}\label{rates2}
|\Delta_t(p,q)|
&\leq&
C't^{-(\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q))}
\sum_{k=1}^{t}
\frac{1}{k^{2-(\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q))}}
\nonumber \\
&=&
\begin{cases}
\mathcal{O}\left(t^{-1}\right),
& \text{if } \operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q)>1,\\
\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log t}{t}\right),
& \text{if } \operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q)=1,\\
\mathcal{O}\left(t^{-(\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q))}\right),
& \text{if } 0<\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q)<1.
\end{cases}
\end{eqnarray}
Also, $\Delta_t(s,s)$ converges to
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(k+1)^2}\beta_k(s,s)
\eqqcolon C$. Then, $\Delta_{t} \to C e_{s}^\top e_{s}$ as $t \to \infty$. Using again $e_s^\top e_sP^{-1}U=0_{N\times N}$, we get that
$\operatorname{Var}(D_{t+1})=\mathcal{O}(t^{-\delta})$ for some $\delta>0$.

label: lem:limit_Z
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:limit_Z}
Assume that {\rm \bf (B)} and {\rm \bf (C)} hold, and suppose that $p_1+p_2=d_1+d_2$. Then $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J$ converges almost surely. If
$\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty$ denotes its almost sure limit, then
\[
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty(Q\widetilde{A}-I)=-\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Under the standing assumption {\rm \bf (A2)}, we have
$\mathbf{1}\widetilde A=\mathbf{1}$. Multiplying the two identities
in {\rm \bf (B)} on the left by $\mathbf{1}$ therefore gives
\[
N\mu_{\mathcal P}^{out}=p_1+p_2,
\qquad
N\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out}=d_1+d_2.
\]
Since $p_1+p_2=d_1+d_2$ and these two quantities sum to $N$,
it follows that
\[
\mu_{\mathcal P}^{out}
=\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out}
=\frac12.
\]
In particular,
$\mu_{\mathcal P}^{out}-\mu_{\mathcal D}^{out}=0<1$.
The final part of Theorem~\ref{thm:AS_average} now implies
that all four block sums
$Z_t^{P_1},Z_t^{P_2},Z_t^{D_1},Z_t^{D_2}$
converge almost surely. Consequently,
\[
Y_t:=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J
=
\frac{Z_t^{P_1}}{p_1}\mathbf{1}_{P_1}
+\frac{Z_t^{P_2}}{p_2}\mathbf{1}_{P_2}
+\frac{Z_t^{D_1}}{d_1}\mathbf{1}_{D_1}
+\frac{Z_t^{D_2}}{d_2}\mathbf{1}_{D_2}
\]
converges almost surely. Denote its limit by $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty$. Note that $H = Q \tilde{A} - I$.
                                                                      
Taking conditional expectations in \eqref{noderecurnew}
and writing the result in vector form gives
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
=
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t+\frac{1}{t+1}\bigl(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH+ \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A \bigr).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:commute}, $\tilde J$ commutes with $H$.
Moreover, {\rm \bf (C)} implies that
$b:=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A$ is constant on each
of the four blocks, so $b\tilde J=b$. Multiplying the
preceding identity on the right by $\tilde J$ yields
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[Y_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
=
Y_t+\frac{1}{t+1}\bigl(Y_tH+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A\bigr).
\]
Thus,
\[
Y_{t+1}
=
Y_t+\frac{1}{t+1} (Y_tH+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A)+\Delta R_{t+1},
\qquad
\Delta R_{t+1}
:=
Y_{t+1}-\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[Y_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t].
\]

The sequence $\{\Delta R_{t+1}\}$ is a martingale
difference sequence. More explicitly, writing
$\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}$ for the row vector of sampling indicators,
\eqref{noderecurnew} gives
$\Delta R_{t+1} = \frac{1}{t+1}
\left(\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}-\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]\right)\widetilde A\tilde J$. Since the indicators are bounded and the matrices are fixed, there is a deterministic constant $C<\infty$
such that $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}\!\left[\|\Delta R_{t+1}\|_2^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t\right]
\leq \frac{C}{(t+1)^2}$. Hence the partial sums of $\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\Delta R_{t+1}$ form an $\mathcal L^2$-bounded martingale and converge almost surely. Summing the recursion for $Y_t$ gives
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{1}{t+1}(Y_tH+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A)
=
Y_{n+1}-Y_0-\sum_{t=0}^{n}\Delta R_{t+1}.
\]
The right-hand side converges almost surely. Therefore
the vector series on the left converges almost surely.
On the other hand,
\[
Y_tH+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A \longrightarrow\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty H+ \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A
\qquad\text{almost surely}.
\]
If any coordinate of this limiting vector were nonzero,
the corresponding coordinate of $Y_tH+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A$ would
eventually have a fixed sign and absolute value bounded
away from zero. Since
$\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}(t+1)^{-1}=\infty$, the corresponding
coordinate series would then diverge, a contradiction.
Thus $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty H+\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A=0$, which is precisely
\[
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty(Q\widetilde A-I)
=-\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We show that $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$ is a quasi-martingale. By Lemma~\ref{lem:limit_Z}, $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J$ converges almost surely. Denote its limit by $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty$. Set $Y_t=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J$, and $\tilde{\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}}_t=Y_t-\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty$. From \eqref{eq:EVar}, \[ \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]-\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t = \frac{1}{t+1}\left[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH+\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}\right]. \] Using $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)H+Y_tH$ and $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty H+\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A=0$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:limit_Z}, we get \[ \mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH+\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A} = \mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)H+\tilde{\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}}_tH. \] Therefore, $\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]-\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\|] \leq \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)H\|]}{t+1} + \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\tilde{\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}}_tH\|]}{t+1}$. We first consider the term $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)H$. We apply Proposition~\ref{prop:Var} with
$H_1=(I-\tilde J)H$. By {\rm \bf (C)}, $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}$ is constant on the four parts of the partition, so $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}\tilde J
=\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}$, and hence
$\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}H_1=0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:commute}, $\tilde J$
commutes with $Q\widetilde A$; since $H=Q\widetilde{A}-I$ also commutes with $Q\widetilde{A}$, we
get $Q\widetilde AH_1=H_1Q\widetilde A$. Finally, since $\hat v$ is constant on the four parts of
the partition, $\hat v\tilde J=\hat v$, and hence $\hat vH_1=0$. Hence Proposition~\ref{prop:Var} gives $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH_1]=\mathcal O(t^{-a_1})$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH_1)=\mathcal O(t^{-b_1})$ for some $a_1,b_1>0$. Thus $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_tH_1\|]=\mathcal O(t^{-c_1})$ for some $c_1>0$. Since $t+1$ grows linearly, \[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)H\|]}{t+1}<\infty. \] For the second term, set
$G_t:=Y_tH+\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:limit_Z}, $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty H+\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}=0$, and hence
$G_t=(Y_t-\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_\infty)H=\tilde{\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}}_tH$. From the recursion for $Y_t$ obtained in
Lemma~\ref{lem:limit_Z},
\[
Y_{t+1} = Y_t+\frac{1}{t+1} \left(Y_tH+\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}\right) +\Delta R_{t+1},
\]
where $\Delta R_{t+1}$ is a martingale difference and
$\sum_t\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\Delta R_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]<\infty$ almost surely. Multiplying the above recursion by $H$
and adding $\mathbf 1_{\mathcal D}\widetilde{A}$ gives
\[
G_{t+1}=G_tK_t+\Delta R_{t+1}H.
\]

Now write $I-Q\widetilde{A}=P\Lambda P^{-1}$, where
$\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_N)$, and choose $s$ such
that $\nu_s=0$. Since
$H=-P\Lambda P^{-1}$, we have
$HPe_s^\top=-P\Lambda e_s^\top=0$. Therefore
$G_tPe_s^\top=0$ and $\Delta R_{t+1}HPe_s^\top=0$. Thus, if $U_t=G_tP$ and
$\xi_{t+1}=\Delta R_{t+1}HP$, then $U_t(s)=\xi_{t+1}(s)=0$, while for
$i\neq s$,
\[
U_{t+1}(i)
= U_t(i)\left(1-\frac{\nu_i}{t+1}\right) + \xi_{t+1}(i).
\]
Since $\operatorname{Re}(\nu_i)>0$ for $i\neq s$ and
$\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\xi_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]=\mathcal O(t^{-2})$, iterating the scalar recursion and using the same Euler-product estimates as in Proposition~\ref{prop:Var} gives
$\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|G_t\|]=\mathcal O(t^{-a_2})$ for some $a_2>0$. Consequently, since
$G_t=\tilde{\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}}_tH$,
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}
\frac{\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\tilde{\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}}_tH\|]}{t+1}
=
\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}
\frac{\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|G_t\|]}{t+1}
<\infty.
\]
Combining the two estimates, we get
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]-\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\|]<\infty.
\]
Since $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$ is bounded, it follows that $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$ is a bounded quasimartingale. Hence $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$ admits an almost sure limit.

label: prop:urn
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:urn}
The normalized interacting urn model satisfies
\eqref{eq:main_recur_vec}, with
$\mu_{ji}=(\alpha_{ji}+\beta_{ji}-m_{ji})/\tilde m_i$
and $c_{ji}=(m_{ji}-\beta_{ji})/\tilde m_i$,
where $\tilde m_i=\sum_{j\in N(i)}m_{ji}$.
The remainder is given in the proof below.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The evolution of the number of white balls is given by
$$W_{t+1}(i)=W_t(i) + \sum_{j \in N(i)}\{ \alpha_{ji} \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) + (m_{ji}-\beta_{ji})(1-\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j))\},$$
where
$\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j)\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t\sim
\operatorname{Ber}\!\left(
(1-q_j)+(2q_j-1)\sum_{k\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}}w_{kj}Z_t(k)
\right)$.
Note that the total number of balls in urn $i$ updates as $T_{t+1}(i)=T_t(i) + \tilde{m}_i$, where $\tilde{m}_i=\sum_{j \in N(i)}m_{ji}$. We get
\begin{eqnarray*}
Z_{t+1}(i)&=
&\frac{Z_t(i)T_t(i)}{T_{t+1}(i)} +\frac{1}{T_{t+1}(i)}\left( \sum_{j \in N(i)}(\alpha_{ji}+\beta_{ji}-m_{ji})\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) +   \sum_{j \in N(i)}(m_{ji}-\beta_{ji} )            \right) \\
&=& Z_t(i)\left(1-\frac{\tilde{m}_i}{T_{t+1}(i)} \right)+\frac{\tilde{m}_i}{T_{t+1}(i)}\left( \sum_{j \in N(i)}\mu_{ji}\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) +   \sum_{j \in N(i)}\frac{m_{ji}-\beta_{ji}}{\tilde{m}_i} \right)
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\mu_{ji}=\frac{\alpha_{ji}+\beta_{ji}-m_{ji}}{\tilde{m}_i}$.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            

Hence,
\begin{align*}
Z_{t+1}(i) &=Z_t(i)\left(1-\frac{\tilde{m}_i}{T_{t+1}(i)} \right)+ \frac{\tilde{m}_i}{T_{t+1}(i)}\Big[ 
\sum_{j \in N(i)} \left(\mu_{ji} \mathbb{E}\left[ \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right] + \frac{m_{ji} - \beta_{ji}}{\tilde{m}_i} \right) + \Delta M_{t+1}(i)\Big]\\
&=Z_t(i)\left(1-\frac{1}{t+1} \right)+ \frac{1}{t+1}\Big[ 
\sum_{j \in N(i)} \left(\mu_{ji} \mathbb{E}\left[ \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right] + \frac{m_{ji} - \beta_{ji}}{\tilde{m}_i} \right) + \Delta M_{t+1}(i) +\epsilon_{t+1}(i)\Big],
\end{align*}
where  $ \mathbb{E}\left[ \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right] =(1 - q_j) + (2q_j - 1) \sum_{k\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}} w_{kj} Z_t(k)$, $\Delta M_{t+1}(i)=\sum_{j \in N(i)} \mu_{ji}\big(\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j)-\mathbb{E}\left[ \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right]\big)$, and
\begin{align*}
\epsilon_{t+1}(i) 
&= \left(\frac{(t+1)\tilde{m}_i}{T_{t+1}(i)}-1\right)\Bigg[ 
\sum_{j \in N(i)} \left(\mu_{ji}\mathbb{E}\left[ \mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{t+1}(j) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right] + \frac{m_{ji} - \beta_{ji}}{\tilde{m}_i} \right)
 + \Delta M_{t+1}(i) - Z_t(i) \Bigg]. \\
 \end{align*}

title: Corollary
body_md:
Suppose that the sampling and reinforcement graphs have the
same underlying strongly connected directed graph.
Then $WQ\widetilde A-I$ is invertible provided at least one
of the following conditions holds.
\begin{itemize}
                                       
                                           
  \item[(i)] There exists $r^* \in [N]$ such that $|2q_{r^*}-1|<1$ and either there exists an odd cycle in the graph or there exists another vertex $r^\prime$ such that $|2q_{r^\prime} - 1|<1$ and $r^* \rightsquigarrow r^\prime$ (or $r^\prime \rightsquigarrow r^*$) via a path of odd length.
  \item[(ii)] There exists a non-P\'olya edge $e_1=(u_1, v_1)$ in the graph and either the graph has an odd cycle or there exists another non-P\'olya edge $e_2 = (u_2, v_2)$ such that $u_1 \rightsquigarrow u_2$ (or $u_2 \rightsquigarrow u_1$) via a path of odd length.
  \item[(iii)] All edges are P\'olya-type and $q_v\in\{0,1\}$ for every $v\in\mbox{${\mathcal V}$}$. $\mbox{${\mathcal G}$}$ contains an odd cycle and does not admit a partition under the GPA.
                                   
\end{itemize}

label: prop:spectral_centering_ZJ
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:spectral_centering_ZJ}
Work with the random-limit model and the fixed GPA partition
of Section~\ref{sec:convergence_random}.
Assume {\bf (B)}, {\bf (C)}, and {\bf (D)} hold. Write\[
I-Q\widetilde A=P\Lambda P^{-1},
\qquad
\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_N),
\]
and let $s$ be such that $\nu_s=0$. If $q_k$ denotes
the $k$-th row of $P^{-1}$, then
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]
=
(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\tilde J]P)_s q_s
+
\sum_{k\neq s}
\frac{(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A P)_k}{\nu_k}\,q_k.

head: environment

label: eq:centering-coordinate
title: Proof
body_md:
From~\eqref{eq:EVar}, Lemma~\ref{lem:commute}, and {\rm \bf(C)}, we get
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\tilde J]
=
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]K_t+\frac1{t+1}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A,\]
where $K_t=I-\frac{1}{t+1}\left(I-Q\tilde{A} \right)$ is as before. For $i\leq j$, let $\Phi_{i,j}=K_iK_{i+1}\cdots K_j$, and let
$\Phi_{i,j}=I$ if $i>j$. Iterating the preceding recursion gives
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]
=
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\tilde J]\Phi_{0,t-1}
+
\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\frac{1}{i+1}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D} \tilde{A} \Phi_{i+1,t-1}.
\]
By {\rm \bf (D)}, $\Phi_{i,j}
=
P\prod_{\ell=i}^{j}
\left(I-\frac{1}{\ell+1}\Lambda\right)P^{-1}$. Multiplying on the right by $P$, we obtain, for every $k$,
\begin{eqnarray}\label{eq:centering-coordinate}
(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]P)_k
=
(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\tilde J]P)_k
\prod_{j=0}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right)
+(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\widetilde A P)_k
\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}
\frac{1}{i+1}
\prod_{j=i+1}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right).
\end{eqnarray}

\noindent For $k=s$, since $\nu_s=0$, \eqref{eq:centering-coordinate} gives
\[
(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]P)_s
=
(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\tilde J]P)_s
+
(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\tilde{A}P)_s
\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\frac{1}{i+1}.
\]
Since $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]P$ is bounded, we must
have $(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\tilde{A}P)_s=0$. Hence $\lim_{t\to\infty}(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]P)_s
= (\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\tilde J]P)_s$. For $k\neq s$, the first term in \eqref{eq:centering-coordinate} converges to
$0$. Moreover,
\[
\frac{1}{i+1}
\prod_{j=i+1}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right)
=
\frac1{\nu_k}
\left[
\prod_{j=i+1}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right)
-
\prod_{j=i}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right)
\right].
\]
Therefore,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}
\frac1{i+1}
\prod_{j=i+1}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right)
= \frac{1}{\nu_k}\left[
1- \prod_{j=0}^{t-1}
\left(1-\frac{1}{j+1}\nu_k\right)
\right].
\]
Since $\operatorname{Re}(\nu_k)>0$, the product on the right converges to
$0$. Hence, for $k\neq s$, $\lim_{t\to\infty}(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]P)_k
=
\frac{(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\tilde{A}P)_k}{\nu_k}$. Writing the limiting row vector in the basis given by the rows
$q_k$ of $P^{-1}$ gives
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t\tilde J]
=
(\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_0\tilde J]P)_s q_s
+
\sum_{k\neq s}
\frac{(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}\tilde{A}P)_k}{\nu_k}\,q_k.
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Define $D_t=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:cycle1}, it is
enough to show that $D_t\to{\bf 0}$ almost surely. We do this in two steps:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $\|D_t\|^2$ admits an almost sure limit.
\item $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|D_t\|^2]\to0$.
\end{enumerate}
Together, these two statements imply $D_t\to{\bf 0}$ almost surely. From \eqref{recur_cycle}, in vector form, and using
\(\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal D}A=\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal P}\), we get
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
=
\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t
\left[
\left(1-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}\right)I
+
\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}QA
\right]
+
\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal P}.
\]
Since $\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal P}(I-\tilde J)=0$ and
$QA(I-\tilde J)=(I-\tilde J)QA$, we get
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_{t+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
=
D_tK_t,
\qquad
K_t:=I-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}(I-QA).
\]

\noindent\textit{Proof of (i).}
Write $D_{t+1}=D_tK_t+\Delta D_{t+1}$, where $\Delta D_{t+1}$ is a martingale
difference. Since the urn increments are bounded and $T_{t+1}$ grows linearly,
there exists a constant $C>0$ such that $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\Delta D_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]\leq \frac{C}{T_{t+1}^2}$. Therefore,
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|D_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
=
\|D_tK_t\|^2+\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|\Delta D_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t].
\]
Since  \(AA^\top=I\), \(QA\) is orthogonal. Using this, we get
\[
I-K_tK_t^\top
=
\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}
\left(1-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}\right)
\{2I-QA-A^\top Q\}
=
\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}
\left(1-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{t+1}}\right)
(I-QA)(I-A^\top Q).
\]
Thus $I-K_tK_t^\top$ is positive semidefinite, and hence $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|D_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
\leq
\|D_t\|^2+\frac{C}{T_{t+1}^2}$.
Since $\sum_tT_{t+1}^{-2}<\infty$, $\|D_t\|^2$ is an almost supermartingale,
and hence admits an almost sure limit.

\ 


\noindent\textit{Proof of (ii).} We show that both $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_t]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(D_t)$ converge to zero.
From the preceding conditional expectation recursion, $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_{t+1}] =
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_0]\prod_{i=0}^{t}K_i$. It is easy to verify that the characteristic polynomial of $QA$ is $x^N-1$. Thus $QA$ is diagonalizable and its eigenvalues are simple. Write
$I-QA=P\Lambda P^{-1}$, where
$\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_N)$.
Let $s$ be such that $\nu_s=0$, and let $e_s$ denote the $s$-th standard row vector. Since the right eigenvector $Pe_s^\top$ corresponding to $\nu_s=0$ is constant on the four parts of the partition, we have
$(I-\tilde J)Pe_s^\top=0$. Hence $D_0Pe_s^\top=0$.
For every $k\neq s$, $\operatorname{Re}(\nu_k)>0$, and Euler's product estimate gives
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{t}
\left(1-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{i+1}}\nu_k\right)
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore $\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_t]\to{\bf 0}$. We now consider the variance.
Let $G_k:=\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\operatorname{Var}(\mbox{${\mathbb I}$}_{k+1}\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_k)]$.
The entries of $G_k$ are uniformly bounded. Applying the
projection $I-\tilde J$ to the recursion for $\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t$, and then
applying the variance decomposition, gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(D_{t+1}) = K_t^\top\operatorname{Var}(D_t)K_t
+ \frac{(\bar m^{in})^2}{T_{t+1}^2}
(I-\tilde J)^\top A^\top G_t A(I-\tilde J).\]
Iterating this recursion, and using the fact that the initial configuration is
deterministic, so that \(\operatorname{Var}(D_0)=0\), gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(D_{t+1}) = \sum_{k=0}^{t} \frac{(\bar m^{in})^2}{T_{k+1}^2} \left(\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}K_i^\top\right)
(I-\tilde J)^\top A^\top G_k A (I-\tilde J) \left(\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}K_i\right),
\]
where an empty product is understood to be the identity matrix. Using the diagonalization of $I-QA$, we have
\[
\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}K_i = P\prod_{i=k+1}^{t} \left(I-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{i+1}}\Lambda\right)P^{-1}.
\]
Thus the corresponding middle term in the eigenbasis has entries of the form
\[
\Delta_t(p,q) = \sum_{k=0}^{t}
\frac{(\bar m^{in})^2}{T_{k+1}^2}
\left[
\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}
\left(1-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{i+1}}\nu_p\right)
\right]
\delta_k(p,q)
\left[
\prod_{i=k+1}^{t}
\left(1-\frac{\bar m^{in}}{T_{i+1}}\nu_q\right)
\right],
\]
where $\delta_k(p,q)$ denotes the $(p,q)$-th entry of
$P^\top (I-\tilde J)^\top A^\top G_k A(I-\tilde J)P$. These entries are uniformly bounded. Moreover,
because $(I-\tilde J)Pe_s^\top=0$, the $s$-th row and the $s$-th column of this middle
matrix are zero. Hence only indices with non-zero eigenvalues contribute.
For $p,q\neq s$, Euler's product estimate gives
\[
|\Delta_t(p,q)|
\leq
C
t^{-(\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q))}
\sum_{k=1}^{t}
\frac{1}{k^{2-(\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q))}}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|\Delta_t(p,q)|
=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal O(t^{-1}),&
\text{if }\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q)>1,\\
\mathcal O((\log t)/t),&
\text{if }\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q)=1,\\
\mathcal O\!\left(t^{-(\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q))}\right),&
\text{if }0<\operatorname{Re}(\nu_p)+\operatorname{Re}(\nu_q)<1.
\end{cases}
\]
Since there are only finitely many indices and all non-zero eigenvalues have
positive real parts, this implies $\operatorname{Var}(D_t)\to0$. Therefore
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|D_t\|^2]
=
\|\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[D_t]\|^2+\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Var}(D_t))
\longrightarrow0.
\]

By (i), $\|D_t\|^2$ has an almost sure limit. Since $D_t$ is bounded and
$\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|D_t\|^2]\to0$, bounded convergence implies that this almost sure limit
is zero. Hence $D_t\to{\bf 0}$ almost surely.

Finally, $D_t=\mbox{${{\mathbf Z}}$}_t(I-\tilde J)\to{\bf 0}$ means that each coordinate
synchronizes with its block average. Combining this with Theorem~\ref{thm:cycle1} we get that as $t \to \infty$, for every $i\in P_1\cup D_2$, $Z_t(i) \xrightarrow{a.s.} \xi_\infty$ and for every $i\in P_2\cup D_1$,
$Z_t(i)\xrightarrow{a.s.} 1-\xi_\infty$.

label: def:sas
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:sas}
A recursion for a sequence $\{x_t\}_{t\geq0}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ of the form
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:recursion}
x_{t+1}
=
x_t+a_t\bigl(h(x_t)+M_{t+1}+\epsilon_{t+1}\bigr),
\qquad t\geq0,
\end{equation}
is called a \emph{stochastic approximation scheme} if it satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)]
The \emph{map} $h\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is Lipschitz.

\item[(2)]
The \emph{step sizes} $\{a_t\}_{t\geq0}$ satisfy $a_t\in(0,\infty)$ for all $t\geq0$, $\sum_{t\geq0}a_t=\infty$, and $\sum_{t\geq0}a_t^2<\infty$.

\item[(3)]
The sequence $\{M_t\}_{t\geq1}$ is a martingale
difference sequence with respect to $\{\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t\}_{t\geq0}$ and, for
some constant $K>0$,
\[
\mbox{${\mathbb E}$}[\|M_{t+1}\|^2\mid\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t]
\leq K(1+\|x_t\|^2)
\qquad \mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
\]

\item[(4)]
The \emph{solution} $\{x_t\}_{t\geq0}$ satisfies $\sup_{t\geq0}\|x_t\|<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.

\item[(5)]
The \emph{errors} $\{\epsilon_t\}_{t\geq1}$ are adapted to the filtration $\{\mbox{${\mathcal F}$}_t\}_{t\geq0}$, are bounded, and satisfy $\epsilon_t\to0$ $\mathbb{P}$-a.s.
\end{enumerate}

label: lem:sas
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sas}
Suppose that conditions~{\rm(1)--(5)} in Definition~\ref{def:sas} hold. Furthermore, suppose that the set of limit points of the solutions to the ODE $y'(u)=h(y(u))$, $u\geq0$, with $y(0)\in\mathbb{R}^d$ coincides with the set of zeroes of $h$, and that these zeroes are isolated. Then the iterates of the recursion in \eqref{eq:recursion} converge $\mathbb{P}$-a.s. to a possibly sample-path-dependent zero of $h$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{aux:MP_compact_LIL}
Consider the stochastic approximation algorithm
\[
Z_{n+1}
=
Z_n+\gamma_n\bigl[h(Z_n)+r_{n+1}\bigr]
+\sigma_n\xi_{n+1},
\]
where $Z_n\in\mbox{${\mathbb R}$}^d$, $\gamma_n>0$, and $\sigma_n>0$. Set $v_n:=\gamma_n/\sigma_n^2$ and $s_n:=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gamma_k$. Assume the following conditions.

\begin{enumerate}
\item[{\bf (1)}]
There exists a deterministic point $z_\star\in\mbox{${\mathbb R}$}^d$ such that $Z_n\to z_\star$ almost surely.

\item[{\bf (2)}]
The function $h$ is differentiable at $z_\star$, and its Jacobian matrix $H:=Dh(z_\star)$ satisfies
\[
\max\{\mathrm{Re}(\mu):\mu\in\mathrm{Sp}(H)\}=-L<0.
\]

\item[{\bf (3)}]
We have $\sigma_n\to0$, $\gamma_n\to0$, $s_n\to\infty$, $\gamma_n/\gamma_{n+1}=1+O(\gamma_n)$, and there exists $\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}\in[0,2L)$ such that
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac1{\gamma_n}
\left(1-\frac{v_{n-1}}{v_n}\right)
=
\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}.
\]

\item[{\bf (4)}]
There exist a positive definite matrix $\Gamma$ and independent $\mathcal N(0,\Gamma)$ random vectors $(\eta_k)_{k\geq1}$ such that
\[
\left\|
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\xi_{k+1}
-
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\eta_{k+1}
\right\|_2
=
o\!\left(
\sqrt{\frac{\log s_n}{\gamma_n}}
\right)
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

\item[{\bf (5)}]
The remainder satisfies $r_{n+1}=r_{n+1}^{(1)}+o(\|Z_n-z_\star\|_2)$ a.s. with $\|r_{n+1}^{(1)}\|_2=O(v_n^{-1/2})$ a.s.
\end{enumerate}

Define
\[
\Sigma
:=
\int_0^\infty
\exp\!\left((H+\tfrac{\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}}{2}I)u\right)^\top
\Gamma
\exp\!\left((H+\tfrac{\rho_{\mathrm{MP}}}{2}I)u\right)
\,du.
\]
Then, with probability one, the sequence
$\left\{\sqrt{v_n/(2\log s_n)}\,(Z_n-z_\star)\right\}_{n\geq1}$
is relatively compact in $\mbox{${\mathbb R}$}^d$, and its set of limit points is the ellipsoid
$\{x\in\mbox{${\mathbb R}$}^d:x\Sigma^{-1}x^\top\leq1\}$.
